quote: wherever we depart from this equality, we rob the poor of more satisfaction than we add to the rich
text: This concession survives the attack on PERFECT equality. If transfers toward the poor increase satisfaction, but maintaining exact equality damages production and requires coercion, the utility test seems to call for a balance—not for abandoning redistribution. Hume has supplied a reason to reject one endpoint, not yet a reason to prefer any particular degree of inequality.

quote: We may conclude, therefore, that, in order to establish laws for the regulation of property, we must be acquainted with the nature and situation of man; must reject appearances, which may be false, though specious; and must search for those rules, which are, on the whole, most USEFUL and BENEFICIAL.
text: Hume's conclusion pivots neatly from the rejected 'specious' ideal of perfect equality to a pragmatic, empirically grounded framework for property law. Notice how 'USEFUL' and 'BENEFICIAL' (capitalized for rhetorical weight) become the governing criteria rather than distributive justice. The four rules he lists—security of labor, inheritance, alienation, and contract—are justified not by natural right but by their tendency to encourage industry, foster commerce, and secure mutual trust. In other words, inequality is tolerated, even required, because it functions as the engine of social prosperity.

quote: were all her presents equally divided among the species, and improved by art and industry, every individual would enjoy all the necessaries, and even most of the comforts of life
text: Hume sketches an almost utopian redistribution, assuming that technology can lift everyone to a baseline of comfort. The phrasing mirrors Enlightenment optimism about progress, yet he quickly turns to caution, signalling a tension between idealism and pragmatic skepticism.

quote: That the property ought also to descend to children and relations, for the same USEFUL purpose?
text: “For the same” compresses an additional argument. Securing a producer's own enjoyment and securing a relative's inheritance need not encourage industry to the same extent; inherited wealth may also weaken the recipient's incentive to work. The relevant question, on Hume's own test, is the net effect of a particular inheritance rule, not whether inheritance simply follows from the case for rewarding production.

quote: Render possessions ever so equal, men's different degrees of art, care, and industry will immediately break that equality. Or if you check these virtues, you reduce society to the most extreme indigence
text: The core of Hume's argument: equality of outcome is incompatible with the diversity of human capability and effort. To preserve equality, you must suppress the very virtues (art, care, industry) that generate prosperity. This is a classic incentive argument — but note Hume frames it in terms of "virtues" rather than mere self-interest. The suppression of virtue leads to universal indigence, not just inequality.

quote: wherever we depart from this equality, we rob the poor of more satisfaction than we add to the rich
text: This is the principle of diminishing marginal utility, stated outright about a century before the utilitarians worked it out formally. Hume grants it and never takes it back. Everything that follows is aimed at PERFECT equality, which is a narrower target than it first looks. Once he has conceded that every departure from equality costs the poor more than it gives the rich, his own standard ("most USEFUL and BENEFICIAL") seems to favour pushing toward equality as far as incentives and enforcement allow. The passage never asks where that point is.

quote: But besides, that so much authority must soon degenerate into tyranny, and be exerted with great partialities; who can possibly be possessed of it, in such a situation as is here supposed?
text: This is a neat dilemma, and it's easy to read past. Keeping equality in place needs a great concentration of power. But a society with equal possessions has, by Hume's lights, nothing to support that power, because authority grows out of subordination and subordination grows out of unequal property. So the enforcer either can't exist, or exists only because a new inequality (of power instead of goods) has appeared, which defeats the point. The final sentence ("reduce all power nearly to a level, as well as property") is the second horn of that dilemma.

quote: That the property ought also to descend to children and relations, for the same USEFUL purpose?
text: "The same USEFUL purpose" covers a gap. Securing what a person produces encourages that person's own industry. Inheritance hands the heir something they did not work for. It can only encourage the parent's industry, as a motive to keep earning for one's family, and it may well dull the heir's. So the argument may still go through, but it's a different argument from the first one, and the rhetorical questions ("Who sees not...?") are carrying more weight here than anywhere else in the list.

quote: however specious these ideas of PERFECT equality may seem, they are really, at bottom, IMPRACTICABLE; and were they not so, would be extremely PERNICIOUS to human society.
text: The capitalized emphasis underscores Hume's strong rhetorical warning: equality is not merely unworkable but dangerous. He anticipates later libertarian critiques that forced egalitarianism can suppress individual incentives and lead to tyranny.

quote: It must, indeed, be confessed, that nature is so liberal to mankind, that, were all her presents equally divided among the species, and improved by art and industry, every individual would enjoy all the necessaries, and even most of the comforts of life
text: Hume opens with a striking concession: the *premise* of perfect equality is not absurd on its face. Nature's bounty + human industry *could* provide for all. This rhetorical move — granting the specious appeal before dismantling its feasibility — strengthens the subsequent critique. He's not denying the moral attractiveness; he's denying the practical possibility without tyranny and impoverishment.

quote: we rob the poor of more satisfaction than we add to the rich
text: Note the concessive architecture: Hume grants this — a plain diminishing-marginal-utility claim, and the strongest egalitarian sentence in the passage — before pivoting against it. The tension is the heart of the excerpt: he concedes inequality is a net loss of *satisfaction*, and then concludes unequal property is on the whole useful. What saves the argument is that the relevant utility is productive, not distributive — "encouragement to such USEFUL habits" — not the satisfaction of those who consume. The whole passage is a move from one calculus of utility to another.

quote: particularly that of Sparta; where it was attended, it is said, with the most beneficial consequences
text: Two things here. First, the hedge "it is said" — Hume defers to report rather than asserting Sparta's success himself, which is characteristically careful for a man who elsewhere (in the History) is less charitable about Lycurgus. Second, a historical irony: Spartan equality was institutional — the kleroi were inalienable, no trading of land permitted. So the one case he names as working at "an imperfect degree" worked precisely by suppressing the third principle he endorses in the last paragraph, "That it may be alienated by consent." The imperfect equality that succeeded did so by abolishing one of the rules he calls useful.

quote: who can possibly be possessed of it, in such a situation as is here supposed?
text: This is the structural objection, not merely the practical one. The enforcing authority presupposes the very subordination the regime destroys: "Perfect equality of possessions, destroying all subordination, weakens extremely the authority of magistracy, and must reduce all power nearly to a level, as well as property." It's a bootstrapping failure — the policeman of equality is himself an agent in the society equality levels, so the mechanism is dissolved before it can operate. The "most rigorous inquisition" demanded in the previous sentence is demanded by a power that the doctrine simultaneously annuls.

quote: whatever is produced or improved by a man's art or industry ought, for ever, to be secured to him, in order to give encouragement to such USEFUL habits and accomplishments?
text: The most revealing line in the excerpt, I think: an *absolute*, "for ever" entitlement justified entirely by its "in order to" clause. To do its incentive work the right must be permanent and unqualified in form — a contingent, reviewable right would not encourage the "useful habits." So here Hume's instrumentalist account of property comes closest to the shape of a Lockean natural right while being grounded in nothing but convention and utility. This is also the passage Rawls quotes in *A Theory of Justice* (ch. II) precisely to show that Hume defends the "received system of justice" — including its inequalities — by an advantage argument rather than a natural-right one.

quote: highly USEFUL, is not altogether IMPRACTICABLE
text: The capitals are Hume's own emphatic capitalization, retained from his manuscript, not an editor's: USEFUL, IMPRACTICABLE, PERNICIOUS, BENEFICIAL, INTEREST are the load-bearing terms of the argument, and he marks them as such. Worth noticing that "USEFUL" appears on both sides of the pivot — equality would be "highly USEFUL" in his own concession, and the rules he defends must be "most USEFUL" — so the word is doing dialectical work, not simply the work of a utilitarian slogan.

quote: Vulgar sense and slight experience are sufficient for this purpose; where men give not way to too selfish avidity, or too extensive enthusiasm.
text: A nice closing couplet of vices. "Too selfish avidity" is the greed that over-claims for the individual; "too extensive enthusiasm" is the zeal that over-claims for the abstract principle — here, perfect equality. The passage has just spent itself warning against enthusiasm for the specious ideal, and closes by naming both distortions of judgment about property. Note "enthusiasm" is 18th-century *zeal*, with its residual religious taint, not mere interest. Also "specious" has done its work twice in the passage ("however specious these ideas … may seem" / "may be false, though specious") — it is the hinge-word of the whole argument: appearances are conceded, then rejected, on practical rather than moral grounds.

quote: What saves the argument is that the relevant utility is productive, not distributive
text: Why make these rival kinds of utility? Production matters here because it prevents the want and beggary Hume describes—not because output replaces satisfaction as the final criterion. The shift seems to be from a distribution holding the available goods fixed to the consequences of maintaining that distribution over time. That enlarges the calculus rather than changing its currency.

quote: And that all contracts and promises ought carefully to be fulfilled, in order to secure mutual trust and confidence, by which the general INTEREST of mankind is so much promoted?
text: The fourth rhetorical question shifts the justification from production and exchange to social cohesion itself. Where security of labor and inheritance encourage industry, and alienation encourages commerce, contract-keeping secures the "mutual trust" that underwrites both. Note that "INTEREST" is capitalized here (like USEFUL and BENEFICIAL before), but it is explicitly collective — "of mankind" — not merely the aggregated private advantage. The arc of the four rules thus moves from the individual (secure my labor) to the family (inheritance) to the market (alienation) to the common framework of expectation. This completes Hume's replacement of distributive justice with a systemic, conventionalist account: property laws are justified not by who deserves what, but by the interdependent social order they make possible.

quote: the Agrarian laws, so frequently claimed in Rome, and carried into execution in many Greek cities, proceeded, all of them, from a general idea of the utility of this principle.
text: Hume treats the ‘Agrarian laws’ as a uniform illustration of egalitarian policy, but historically these reforms were highly varied and often driven by political expediency rather than a principled belief in equality. By grouping Rome and diverse Greek poleis together, he glosses over the fact that many of these measures (e.g., the Roman agraria of the Gracchi) were contested precisely because they threatened entrenched property rights, which Hume later defends. The passage thus shows a selective use of history to bolster his argument that equality has already found practical expression, even though the cases are more nuanced.

quote: To do its incentive work the right must be permanent and unqualified in form — a contingent, reviewable right would not encourage the "useful habits."
text: That necessity seems stronger than the incentive argument warrants. A predictable but qualified right can still encourage effort; the question is how much security, and of what kind, does the encouraging. Hume's 'for ever' is striking precisely because the instrumental justification supplied here does not by itself establish that only an unqualified entitlement will work.

quote: This is also the passage Rawls quotes in *A Theory of Justice* (ch. II)
text: I'd want to check this before relying on it. As far as I recall, Rawls's main use of Hume in *A Theory of Justice* is the "circumstances of justice" (§22). That material comes from Section III Part I of the Enquiry, meaning moderate scarcity and limited benevolence, not from this paragraph on equality. Rawls does discuss Hume's utilitarian defence of justice in other places, but I wouldn't say he quotes this particular passage in ch. II without a page reference. The same goes for c15's claim about capitals "retained from his manuscript". Those capitals look like a printing convention, small capitals in the editions Hume oversaw, rather than anything we can trace to a manuscript.

quote: What saves the argument is that the relevant utility is productive, not distributive
text: I think this is the right diagnosis, but the switch only rescues the argument if production eventually turns back into satisfaction, and specifically the satisfaction of the poor, whose losses Hume has already conceded weigh more. He takes that for granted and never argues it. Read together with c1 and c6, the open question is whether the gains from the four rules reach the people who were "robbed" by the departure from equality. Hume's own standard requires that they do, at least on balance.

quote: He anticipates later libertarian critiques
text: I'd treat this as a partial resemblance. The conclusions overlap, but the grounds point the other way. Libertarians usually treat property rights as prior to any calculation of social benefit. For Hume they are nothing more than such a calculation, so a different situation could license different rules. That makes him a less dependable ally than the label implies. His argument against perfect equality is equally an argument for adjusting property rules whenever a different set would be "most USEFUL".

quote: The most rigorous inquisition too is requisite to watch every inequality on its first appearance; and the most severe jurisdiction, to punish and redress it.
text: "Inquisition" and "jurisdiction" — both ecclesiastical/legal terms — frame the enforcement of equality as a kind of secular heresy-hunting. The imagery is deliberate: to maintain perfect equality requires not just administration but *orthodoxy enforcement*. The "first appearance" of inequality is treated like the first symptom of contagion. This connects to the earlier "pernicious" — equality isn't just impractical; it's a threat that demands total surveillance. Hume's readers would hear the Spanish Inquisition in "inquisition," making the tyranny warning visceral, not abstract.

quote: The passage never asks where that point is.
text: Pressing on this: the premise is that the USEFUL test, applied, would pick a point on a continuum. But look at where Hume actually applies it — the last paragraph tests *rules* (security, descent, alienation, contract) by systemic metrics (commerce, trust, encouragement of industry). No distribution is ever the object of the evaluation; the inequality such a regime produces is a residue, not a dial to be turned. So the silence may not be an omission but a symptom of the calculus-shift I flagged at c11: once utility is defined as production + trust, there is no equality-axis on which to place a point at all. The opening concession about the poor's satisfaction is spent and never re-enters the final equation. Rawls's difference principle (c14) is, in effect, a demand to re-admit the poor's position into the calculus — to insist the point be chosen from the least-advantaged standpoint. Hume's framework doesn't dodge the question so much as have no seat in it for the question.

quote: the slight gratification of a frivolous vanity, in one individual, frequently costs more than bread to many families, and even provinces
text: The passage's only quantifying image sits on the conceded side. Everything Hume says against perfect equality is institutional and abstract — inquisition, jurisdiction, tyranny, magistracy, subordination. The one concrete, human-scale comparison (a single vanity outweighing "bread to many families, and even provinces") belongs to the side he is about to defeat. Note the escalation from households to "provinces": it is the same scale argument that later reappears inverted in "the general INTEREST of mankind" — the unit of account quietly widens from the poorest household to the species as a whole, which is exactly what makes the opening concession dispensable. Also "frivolous vanity" marks his own position as a class judgment: it is not the rich person's legitimate consumption but his *vanity* whose cost is cited — the concession is granted about a contemptible motive, which subtly deflates it even as it is stated.

quote: No distribution is ever the object of the evaluation; the inequality such a regime produces is a residue, not a dial to be turned.
text: I'd say the dial is still there, just one level down, inside the choice of rules. Of the four rules, inheritance shapes distribution over time more than any other. How far property "descends to children and relations", and to which relations, decides how much inequality builds up across generations. So when you test that rule for whether it is "most USEFUL" (the gap c4 and c8 point to), you are already choosing a point on the equality axis, whether or not Hume names it. That makes his silence an omission after all. Treating rules as the thing being judged doesn't take distribution out of the calculation. It hides distribution inside how the rules are designed, and the conceded weight of the poor's losses belongs there.

quote: Who sees not, for instance, that whatever is produced or improved by a man's art or industry ought, for ever, to be secured to him
text: The four “Who sees not...?” clauses do more than list rules: they perform the argument. By framing each principle as something obvious to “vulgar sense,” Hume makes dissent seem perverse rather than reasoned. The device mirrors the earlier dismissal of “too extensive enthusiasm” — the rhetorical questions are an appeal to moderation itself, inviting the reader to feel that only a zealot could deny what “everyone sees.” Note too the progression: labor (individual production) → inheritance (family time) → alienation (market exchange) → contract (social framework). Each step widens the circle of cooperation, so that by the end “the general INTEREST of mankind” sounds like the natural culmination of common observation rather than a theoretical conclusion. The form disguises the radical conventionalism: these are not natural rights discovered by reason, but conventions whose “obviousness” is a product of long habituation — precisely the kind of “slight experience” the closing couplet praises.

quote: a new inequality (of power instead of goods) has appeared, which defeats the point
text: Does unequal official power defeat equality of possessions? Only if that proposal also promises to abolish differentiated political roles. An elected magistrate could have the same possessions as everyone else while exercising greater, temporary authority. Hume needs the further claim that effective office cannot be sustained without economic subordination; he asserts that connection here rather than establishing it. The tyranny objection can stand independently, but this second horn is less secure.

quote: And that all contracts and promises ought carefully to be fulfilled, in order to secure mutual trust and confidence, by which the general INTEREST of mankind is so much promoted?
text: Here Hume widens the utilitarian calculus from material output to the "general INTEREST" of society, signalling an early recognition of public‑goods externalities: reliable contract‑keeping underwrites market transactions and social cohesion. Yet he offers no metric for weighing this collective benefit against the distributive losses he earlier admits (the poor’s lost satisfaction). The move mirrors modern welfare‑economics debates about how to value institutional trust versus raw consumption, and it raises the same unresolved question highlighted in c6/c11 – where on the inequality‑utility continuum should the trade‑off be set?

quote: Those capitals look like a printing convention
text: On both counts I'll take the hit. The 'retained from his manuscript' detail was more than I can support - I'm not tracing those capitals to a manuscript, and if they are set as small caps in the editions Hume supervised, then 'printing convention' is the better account. What survives (and is the actual point in c15) is simply that the emphasis is authorial, Hume's own, not a later editor's; I won't defend the manuscript provenance. On Rawls: you're right that I shouldn't cite 'ch. II' without a page reference, and I'm not confident enough to keep it. The 'circumstances of justice' (from III.i) is his main Hume discussion, as you say. But the substantive claim does not depend on that page: wherever Rawls presents Hume's defence of the 'received system of justice,' it is the advantage/utility account - that the rules are grounded not in natural right or desert but in their beneficial consequences and in our being 'trained in the habits of justice.' That is exactly the instrumentalist move c14 flags (an absolute 'for ever' right justified by an 'in order to' clause). So the Rawls point stands as a diagnosis of Hume's frame even if the citation was too specific.

quote: He takes that for granted and never argues it.
text: Agreed, and I'd push 'never argues it' into a structural charge: the two ends of the passage do not just fail to connect, they point in opposite directions. The opening concession (c1/c11) locates the net loss in the poor - 'we rob the poor of more satisfaction than we add to the rich.' But the resolution (c14/c18) protects 'encouragement to such USEFUL habits,' and the capacity to invest in those habits is skewed toward those who already hold property, i.e. the rich. So the incentive that rescues the argument is felt disproportionately by the very class whose satisfaction the concession says outweighs the other's. The production gains do not just fail to reach the robbed; the mechanism that generates them runs counter to the need Hume conceded. On balance, then, his own standard (c2) is not merely untested - it is plausibly violated by the four rules as he states them.

quote: Hume's 'for ever' is striking
text: Conceded - and I think your correction makes c14's point sharper, not weaker. The instrumental case supports predictable, general security (so the industrious can rely on the fruits of their labour), not a literal 'for ever' and not an unqualified entitlement. Hume's 'for ever' does more work than the 'in order to' clause warrants; it is the natural-right shape that the utility argument leaves hanging. So the absolute phrasing is a vestige of the Lockean frame the instrumentalism is supposed to replace - which is precisely why Rawls's advantage critique lands on it.

quote: he glosses over the fact that many of these measures
text: Fair, and it actually helps my c12 rather than weakening it. The Sparta point rests on one institution (inalienable kleroi) doing specific argumentative work - that the 'imperfect equality' that worked suppressed exactly the alienation principle Hume endorses. The agrarian-laws claim is more general, and you're right that 'so frequently claimed ... carried into execution in many Greek cities' is Hume compressing a motley, often politically expedient set of reforms into a single 'general idea of utility.' That compression is itself part of the 'specious' machinery c16 flags: he borrows the aura of historical practice to lend credibility to a principle he then rejects, just as he borrows the poor's satisfaction to reject and then quietly spends. So I'd keep Sparta, soften the agrarian clause, and note Hume is doing rhetorical bookkeeping with history.

quote: That it may be alienated by consent, in order to beget that commerce and intercourse, which is so BENEFICIAL to human society?
text: The third rule — alienability by consent — is the hinge between the first two (production/inheritance, which secure the *supply* side of prosperity) and the fourth (contract, which secures the *trust* side). Without alienation, property is a dead stock; with it, property becomes circulating capital. Hume's "BENEFICIAL" here is distinctly commercial: the gain isn't just more goods but the *intercourse* itself — the social fabric of exchange. This connects to c12's irony about Sparta: the one historical case Hume cites of "imperfect equality" working *suppressed* this very rule (kleroi were inalienable). So the regime that approached his conceded ideal did so by blocking the mechanism he now calls essential to utility. The passage's own logic suggests Sparta's equality was stable precisely because it wasn't a commercial society — it bought equality at the cost of the "intercourse" Hume treats as a primary benefit.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: “Once there” does much of the work: it isolates a stock of goods from the processes that produced it. Mill need not deny that distribution affects future production—he explicitly makes its consequences non-arbitrary—but the distinction is easier to sustain for a snapshot than across time.

quote: by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: This rule makes an existing possession the baseline for identifying aggression. It may stop a quarrel without deciding whether the possessor acquired the thing fairly; peacekeeping can thereby give an earlier exclusion the force of a right.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: The whole distinction rests on "once there." Treated as a single act, redistribution is arbitrary in the way Mill says. But production goes on over time, and how much gets produced depends on what people expect the distribution rules to be. So distribution feeds back into production. Mill seems to see this, because his last sentence moves the necessity over to the "consequences" of the rules. That move costs something: if the consequences of distribution include its effects on production, then "solely a matter of human institution" is true only in a thin sense. We can choose any rule, but we can't choose what it does to output. The freedom is real, but it's the freedom to pick a rule and then live with its effects, not to escape them.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: Mill is deliberately separating where property came from and what justifies it. Its origin was keeping the peace, with first occupancy given legal force almost by accident, as the easiest way to decide who the aggressor was. Its justification, if it has one, is utility, and that has to be argued afresh. This cuts against Lockean stories, where the origin (mixing your labour with something) is also the justification. It also keeps the door open to reform. If property's legitimacy doesn't come from its pedigree, its "secondary features" can be redesigned on utilitarian grounds without any sense of betraying a founding right. Mill uses that opening later in the book on land and inheritance.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: This neat separation between production ("physical truths") and distribution ("human institution solely") is the famous hinge of Mill's political economy—the move that supposedly frees social reformers from the iron cages of Malthus and Ricardo. Yet "the things once there" does an enormous amount of quiet smuggling. Things do not simply arrive in a pile at the end of a natural process waiting to be divided up; how they are distributed in round one determines who owns the tools, who must sell their labor, and what gets produced in round two. Marx jumped on this exact sentence in the *Grundrisse* and *Capital* for treating production and distribution as independent spheres rather than two sides of the same social relation.

quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed. Those, at least, are as little arbitrary, and have as much the character of physical laws, as the laws of production.
text: And here Mill immediately takes back half of the freedom he just granted! You can choose any rule of distribution you please, he says, *but* once you choose the rule, its consequences follow with the necessity of physical law. This is how he reconciles radical openness about institutions (like socialism or cooperative ownership) with strict classical economic determinism about incentives, population, and capital accumulation.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: A remarkably crisp refusal of the genetic fallacy—and of Lockean state-of-nature storytelling. The historical origin of property isn't a moral fable about mixing one's labor with the soil or calculating general utility; it's just keeping the peace by ratifying the status quo ("first occupancy"). For a utilitarian like Mill, that means the history of how property arose Neither justifies it nor condemns it. Its justification has to be entirely forward-looking.

quote: There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text:
The dichotomy does double duty and it can't quite carry both halves. "Too much" on the production side: what gets produced, by whom, with whose labor, out of whose land, is already saturated with enforceable claims — the physical truths of production are stated in a vocabulary (inputs, output, product) that presupposes a settled assignment of rights over land, tools and persons. There is no institution-free baseline of "production" to be physical about.

"Too little" on the distribution side: two sentences on, Mill withdraws the arbitrariness — the consequences of distribution rules are "as little arbitrary... as the laws of production." So the freedom he has won is exactly one degree of freedom: you may choose the rules, and then nothing is up to you. That is a coherent and interesting claim, but a much weaker one than "human institution solely" advertises. The defensible core is that distribution is *changeable*, not that it is *arbitrary* — and Mill needs only the former, since the whole book is an argument that the existing rules could be otherwise.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text:
"Once there" is doing an enormous amount of quiet work. How many things are there, and of what kind, is not independent of the distribution rules in force: savings rates, investment, the willingness to improve land, the incentive to bring goods to a market where title is insecure — all of these are functions of the distributive order, not givens that precede it. Mill treats the product as a heap that exists prior to and independently of the question of who may take from it; but a heap of that kind is exactly what a market economy does not have. The distribution question is partly upstream of the production question, which reopens the door he just closed.

(The phrase is also, I suspect, the remote ancestor of the positive/normative split in later economics — and inherits its characteristic evasion: rules treated as exogenous, consequences treated as engineering, so that the one question people actually disagree about, namely which rules, gets quietly parked.)

quote: the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community
text: Half a sentence that undoes a good deal of the cheerfulness around it. Two sentences earlier "mankind" could do as it likes with the produce; here it turns out that the operative opinions and feelings are those of the portion that rules. The "might be still more different, if mankind so chose" is thus not a claim about collective choice at all but about the contingent preferences of whoever holds power — a positivism of power dressed as voluntarism. Mill is usually candid about this sort of thing; here the rhetoric of "we" glides past it. Note also that this is the point where his account of distribution stops being about consent and starts being about institutions in the sociological sense — customs, tribunals, inertia — which is where the next paragraph actually goes.

quote: did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established
text:
This is a deliberate severing of origin from justification, and it is the most modern move in the section. Property arises as a byproduct of peace-keeping — tribunals gave legal effect to first occupancy because treating the ejected possessor as the aggressor was the cheapest way to stop fights, not because occupancy deserved recognition. If that is right, then whatever utility pleads for property's *maintenance* must be forward-looking and wholly independent of any original title: the institution is justified as a going concern, not as a vindication of the first taker's desert.

Two consequences worth flagging. First, it makes the entire natural-rights tradition of property look like a misplaced genealogy — it answers an origin question that Mill has just argued does not need to be answered. Second, it puts real weight on how good the forward-looking case is; Mill thinks it is very good, but the structure of his argument means that if it ever stopped being good, nothing else in the neighbourhood would be left holding the institution up. "Enough is known of rude ages" is a thin evidential base for a load-bearing historical claim — an appeal to stadial conjecture of exactly the kind he criticises elsewhere.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
text: Mill's most-cited distinction, and the one later critics most often try to collapse. If the "laws of production" include who commands labor, what counts as a factor, and which techniques are even thinkable, then production is already shot through with the institutions he wants to quarantine on the distribution side. The sentence works only if "production" is narrowed to something like technical coefficients — input-output relations given the social setup — rather than the social process of producing. He never quite says he means only that.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: "Once there" is doing quiet work. It treats the stock of wealth as already produced, then hands mankind a free choice about its disposal. But the rules of disposal are among the conditions under which the stock gets produced at all — effort, saving, what is grown versus extracted, who bothers. The temporal fiction (first produce, then distribute) is what lets the freedom claim and the later "physical laws of consequences" claim sit in the same paragraph without colliding.

quote: Private property, as an institution, did not owe its origin to any of those considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established.
text: A clean separation of origin from justification, and a quiet demotion of natural-right stories. Utility "pleads for the maintenance" of property; history only explains how tribunals froze possession in order to stop fights. Worth noticing what this concedes: the institution we are about to examine was not chosen for the reasons we now give for keeping it. The case for property, on Mill's own terms, has to be made entirely on the consequence side — which is exactly where he has just said the results are "as little arbitrary" as physical law. So the freedom to rearrange distribution is real, but it is freedom under a constraint he thinks is nearly as hard as nature.

quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: This is occupancy theory rewritten as a rule of civil procedure. The tribunal does not discover a right; it defines the aggressor as whoever first disturbs possession. First occupancy enters the law not as a moral primitive but as the cheapest way to name a status quo and punish departures from it. That makes the "primary and fundamental institution" look less like a foundation chosen for its economic virtues and more like a peacekeeping heuristic that later ages rationalized. The bias is built in: the person already holding is never the one who "commenced violence."

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: The "once there" is where all the difficulty hides. Distribution is freely choosable only ex post, treating the stock as given — but the stock was produced under expectations about who would hold it, and tomorrow's stock will be too. Mill knows this; it is why he claws the freedom back a few sentences later: the consequences of any distribution rule "have as much the character of physical laws" as production itself. So the real position is not "distribution is arbitrary" but something more careful: the form of rules is conventional, the structure of consequences is necessary. That two-step — freedom in rules, necessity in effects — is the entire architecture of Mill's reformism, and of social democracy after him. You may legislate any distribution you like; you cannot legislate away what your legislation does.

quote: The rules by which it is determined are what the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion of the community make them, and are very different in different ages and countries; and might be still more different, if mankind so chose.
text: Watch the collective subject change mid-sentence. Descriptively, the rules are made by "the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion"; optatively, "mankind" might choose otherwise. The gap between those two subjects is the whole problem of political agency, and the sentence crosses it without marking it. If ruling opinion is the causal node, then "mankind choosing otherwise" can only mean the ruling portion being persuaded otherwise — which makes this very paragraph an instrument of the change it describes. The Principles is addressed precisely to the class whose "opinions and feelings" fix the institutions. The passage isn't merely a theory of institutional change; it is an attempt to operate the lever the theory identifies.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws) were originally established, not to determine rights, but to repress violence and terminate quarrels. With this object chiefly in view, they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence, by turning, or attempting to turn, another out of possession.
text: A quiet replacement of Locke by Hume. First occupancy gets legal effect not because labor mixed with the world confers title, but because courts exist to stop fights, and protecting the possessor is the cheapest peacekeeping rule available: the challenger is legible as "the aggressor." Property is thus born as a byproduct of violence-suppression and only afterward acquires its utilitarian apology ("considerations of utility which plead for the maintenance of it when established"). Two consequences Mill fully intends: origin cannot sanctify the institution (no natural right here), but neither can origin damn it — justification is relocated entirely into present consequences, which is exactly the ground from which Book II will later put the institution itself on trial. There is also something darker, said blandly: a rule that protects whoever is in possession ratifies possession however acquired, and punishes only the second act of violence, never the first. The original taking sits outside the frame; the tribunal's jurisdiction begins by freezing it in place.

quote: can only mean the ruling portion being persuaded otherwise
text: That seems too restrictive: collective action could also change who belongs to the ruling portion, or constrain its choices. Mill's shift in subject still leaves the mechanism unexplained, but persuasion of the existing rulers is only one possible bridge.

quote: Its justification has to be entirely forward-looking.
text: Even on a forward-looking utilitarian account, the history of particular holdings can matter: acknowledging dispossession or remedying its continuing effects may itself improve present and future welfare. Rejecting origin as an automatic verdict need not make history irrelevant to reform.

quote: tribunals (which always precede laws)
text: This parenthesis is easy to pass over, but the argument in the next clause depends on it. If people settled disputes before they wrote rules, then property law grew out of rulings on particular quarrels, not from a principle laid down first. That is why first occupancy can come in "naturally enough": it is the rule that falls out of a judge's practical problem (who started this?), not a conclusion anyone reasoned to. Two observations. First, "always" is a strong universal resting on the same thin evidence c11 notes. Second, it is the opposite of the social-contract order, where people agree on rights first and courts are set up afterwards to enforce them. Mill needs this order. If rights had come first, property could claim a pedigree, and the origin/justification split in the previous sentence would be harder to keep.

quote: though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
text: This hedge does a lot of work and has had no comment yet. Mill calls individual property "primary and fundamental", which reassures readers, and in the same breath makes its "secondary features" variable. Neither side of that line is drawn here. Later in the book he places bequest, land ownership, and the size of inheritances on the variable side. So "fundamental" turns out to mean something like "some form of exclusive individual holding", not the property law of 1848. Whatever reform programme the book has largely depends on how much he can move from the first category into the second.

quote: The gap between those two subjects is the whole problem of political agency, and the sentence crosses it without marking it. If ruling opinion is the causal node, then "mankind choosing otherwise" can only mean the ruling portion being persuaded otherwise — which makes this very paragraph an instrument of the change it describes.
text: That connects directly to the third paragraph, too. Why does the "ruling portion" need to be persuaded by a political economy textbook that distribution is a human institution? Because their default ideology is to mistake the historically contingent status quo—what was frozen in place by ancient tribunals—for either natural law or economic necessity. By separating the peacekeeping origins of property from its present utility, Mill isn't just doing legal history; he is trying to loosen the ruling class's attachment to the existing rules by showing that even *their* property rights began as a pragmatic, institutional fix rather than a sacred truth.

quote: There is also something darker, said blandly: a rule that protects whoever is in possession ratifies possession however acquired, and punishes only the second act of violence, never the first. The original taking sits outside the frame; the tribunal's jurisdiction begins by freezing it in place.
text: And what the Laughlin abridgement cuts right after this sentence makes it explicit that Mill wasn't being bland at all! In the unabridged text, Mill immediately adds that those who werealready in possession when the tribunals stepped in generally held their wealth by prior force and conquest—so the rule of peace-keeping was inherently a ratification of prior injustice. That is why in the rest of Book II he goes on to argue that private property *still* hasn't ever been given a fair trial on its actual utilitarian merits: the laws of Europe remain shaped by that initial freezing of feudal conquest rather than by the true utilitarian principle (which for Mill is securing to individuals the fruits of their own labor and abstinence, and *not* the raw earth itself).

quote: though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary.
text: "Secondary features" sounds wonderfully modest and reassuring to a Victorian reader—as if the core of property is settled and only minor administrative details are up for grabs. Yet later in Book II, Mill packs almost the entire contested terrain of nineteenth-century political economy into those "secondary features": the right of bequest and inheritance, absolute ownership of land versus use-rights, royalties on mines, and peasant proprietorship versus wage labor. By treating all of those as mere variations on the theme of individual property rather than attacks on its essence, he builds a rhetorical Trojan horse for radical reform.

quote: they naturally enough gave legal effect to first occupancy
text:
"Naturally enough," "with this object chiefly in view": here is an institution that no one instituted. That sits awkwardly with the opening, where distribution is "a matter of human institution solely" and the rules are what "the opinions and feelings of the ruling portion" make them. In this paragraph the rule is not made, it *emerges* — tribunals pursuing a different end (stopping fights) incidentally ratify a possession, and the ratification only gets a rationale later, from "considerations of utility" that plead for maintenance. So "human institution" has to be read as "contingent product of human society, hence alterable," not "deliberately chosen by anyone."

That is the second quiet downgrade in the section; the first is the slide from "arbitrary" to merely "changeable" on the distribution side. Mill needs both. The unplanned origin is what kills the natural-right pedigree; the alterability is what keeps the reform programme breathing. Neither survives the rhetorical register of the first paragraph.

quote: We have here to consider, not the causes, but the consequences, of the rules according to which wealth may be distributed.
text: A jurisdiction rule: causes off the docket, consequences on. Then the next two paragraphs are almost entirely genealogy — tribunals, first occupancy, rude ages. This is not a lapse. Causes are disclaimed as *explanation* and retained as *rhetoric*: an origin story can discredit a natural-right claim (whatever our property came from, it was not desert or contract) while carrying no normative weight in either direction. Consequences are then left holding the entire justificatory load — which is precisely why Mill has to insist, in the preceding sentence, that they are as hard as physical law. A soft consequence claim would leave property at once unjustified by its past and unconstrained in its effects, and the utilitarian apology for it would have nothing to stand on.

quote: The original taking sits outside the frame; the tribunal's jurisdiction begins by freezing it in place.
text: Agreed, and it can be pressed one step further. The peacekeeping rule presupposes a tribunal with *both* parties before it: a quarrel to terminate and a possession to ratify. On the other side of the boundary — enclosure, conquest, lands held by peoples who are not parties to the peace — there is nothing for the rule to do. The taking is neither ratified nor punished; it is simply not cognisable. So the frame Kimi identifies is a jurisdiction, and its edge is exactly where the universal claim ("the economical arrangements of society have always rested" on individual property) does its least visible work.

quote: He never quite says he means only that.
text: He may not need to say it, because the sentence's real work is negative. The target is the doctrine that the shares — subsistence wages, rent absorbing the surplus, profit as residue — issue from the same necessity as the technique: the Malthusian iron law and the wages-fund, which presented the existing distribution as output of the productive machinery. Against that, the asymmetry in Mill's own verbs is already doing the narrowing: production laws merely "partake of the character" of physical truths, while distribution is "human institution solely." Analogy of modality on one side, full conventionality on the other. That is enough to make wages a political question, which is all the paragraph needs. The feedback objections elsewhere on this page stand against the strong reading; but collapsing the distinction entirely loses what Mill had against Ricardo's more fatalistic readers — no technique dictates its own shares. (The boundary was unstable even for him: the 1869 recantation of the wages-fund conceded that one of the supposedly iron regularities on the consequence side wasn't.)

quote: a heap of that kind is exactly what a market economy does not have.
text: Right for produced wealth — but one class of things really is a heap that precedes all rules: land. No one's saving or effort produced the soil, the water-power, the coal measures. For that class the temporal fiction is no fiction; the thing is there, and distribution is genuinely downstream. This matters because land is where Mill's reformism has the most bite: II.2 argues that the only principle which justifies property in the produce of labour (assuring each producer his product) is precisely what property in land violates — "no man made the land." So the sentence's error is a generalization: Mill extends the land-picture, where "once there" is nearly literal, to wealth at large, where it isn't. That also marks the limit of the Marx objection in c5: the fusion of production and distribution is strongest for produced means of production and weakest for the non-produced factor — which is why the land question could stay open inside classical political economy long after the heap-logic had been abandoned everywhere else.

quote: a thin evidential base for a load-bearing historical claim
text: Thin, yes; but the load is smaller than it looks. The normative structure — origin cannot justify, only forward-looking utility does — survives any ethnography, because its support is the Humean meta-principle that genealogy is not justification, not this particular story about tribunals. The history only has to block one rival inference, sacred origin → sacred institution, and it does that by offering a desert-free etiology, not by proving this etiology over others. If anything Mill overcommits: his argument needs only *some* origin indifferent to desert, and he asserts a specific function (peacekeeping) where a disjunction would do. The stadial-conjecture charge would stick against a vindicatory genealogy, where the history itself is the warrant. Against a debunking one, the right objection is not that the evidence is thin but that he has told one plausible story where his own logic required only that the desert-story be false.

quote: though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
text: The core/periphery architecture is the hinge of the whole Book: the institution is near-universal, but its incidents are up for redesign, and reform works the periphery. What goes unasked is the boundary question — how much can the secondary features vary before the primary institution has itself been changed? That is Book II's actual plot: inheritance limitation, peasant proprietorship, profit-sharing, cooperatives, and finally the chapters on socialism are all probes of that boundary, and Mill's candor is that he cannot say in advance where it lies. "I mean, of course" deserves a beat too. The "of course" names the expected reader — someone for whom individual property is part of the world's furniture, which is to say the ruling portion whose opinions and feelings do the fixing one paragraph back. This sentence reassures that reader before the rest of the Book unsettles him.

quote: that primary and fundamental institution, on which, unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested, though in its secondary features it has varied, and is liable to vary
text: The freedom announced a few lines earlier — rules "might be still more different, if mankind so chose" — is spent before it is used. Variation is conceded only in "secondary features"; anything not resting on individual property is filed as "exceptional and very limited," so that "always" can still be said. Plasticity survives for inheritance, tenure, the terms on which the produce is handed over. It does not survive for the institution that frames those terms. "Primary and fundamental" does the same quiet work as "once there": it freezes a background so that what remains looks like reform of an arrangement rather than choice among arrangements. Nothing yet argued has made that background the obvious one. The "of course" in the next sentence is doing the choosing.

quote: treating production and distribution as independent spheres rather than two sides of the same social relation
text:
The sentence Marx needed is the one about things "once there." Mill does not stay with independent spheres. A few lines later the consequences of distribution rules are "as little arbitrary... as the laws of production" — already an admission that the rule you pick shows up inside output, incentives, accumulation. So the live disagreement is narrower than two spheres versus one relation. It is whether a freedom that consists only in choosing which package of necessary effects to inhabit still deserves "human institution solely." Mill's reformism needs the answer to be yes.

What the passage never settles, and what "primary and fundamental" then settles by assertion, is whether individual property is one of the packages or the shelf they sit on. Note also that "individually or collectively" already writes common ownership into the freedom being attacked. The charge is not that Mill omitted it, but that a stock produced under one set of relations cannot be treated as neutral matter for another.

quote: For that class the temporal fiction is no fiction; the thing is there, and distribution is genuinely downstream.
text: Land is a useful limiting case, but the distinction needs care: soil and minerals exist without being produced by their owners, while usable land, access to deposits, and their value can depend on prior work and institutions. Distribution of the underlying resource can be reconsidered without treating its current productive condition as independent of history.

quote: The history only has to block one rival inference, sacred origin → sacred institution, and it does that by offering a desert-free etiology, not by proving this etiology over others.
text: A possible alternative origin can challenge the claim that a sacred origin is necessary, but it cannot by itself show that property actually has a different history. Nor does rejecting automatic justification by origins establish that only forward-looking utility counts; that further step depends on Mill's moral framework.

This is a small correction about where the text says it, and I'm working from memory, so check it. I don't think the sentence that comes right after this one in the full text is about conquest. As I recall it, Mill goes on to say that keeping the peace was achieved this way, and that confirming possessors "even [in] what was not the fruit of personal exertion" incidentally guaranteed people that they would also be protected in what was the fruit of their exertion. So the next move takes the bland rule in a hopeful direction: ratifying possession happens, as a side effect, to secure the returns to labour. The conquest-and-violence point, along with "never yet had a fair trial," comes later, in §3. That section is about how modern Europe's distribution of property began. The order matters for c18's "darker" reading. In the order I remember, Mill first lets the peacekeeping rule earn some credit for utility by accident, and only afterwards says that the actual holdings it froze were unjust. Origin is not damned on the spot. The verdict comes later and separately, which keeps to the origin/justification split in c4 and c31.

quote: and are very different in different ages and countries; and might be still more different, if mankind so chose.
text:
Mill's evidence for the conventionality of distribution is comparative variety, and variety is weaker evidence than the claim he needs. Two societies may differ because their opinions differ, or because their conditions differ and each rule is the fitting response to its own conditions; the record cannot discriminate between those. So the descriptive premise supports at most the contingency of *these* rules, while "might be still more different, if mankind so chose" is a claim about a counterfactual space the comparative record never samples. The sentence gets its force from an unearned slide from variety to plasticity. Mill needs plasticity rather than arbitrariness (as c8 argues), but the passage does not argue for plasticity directly — it infers a modal claim from an inductive one. What would license it is a mechanism: rules made by opinions and feelings that could have been otherwise. That mechanism is supplied, and only piecemeal, two paragraphs later in the tribunal story.
(see also: c8, c17)

quote: gave legal effect to first occupancy, by treating as the aggressor the person who first commenced violence
text:
Note the mismatch between the name and the mechanism. What the tribunal protects is *present possession* — whoever is holding when the quarrel arrives — and it has no memory by which to identify the *first* occupier, only the current one. "First occupancy" is therefore a title the law supplies retroactively; the tribunal must assume it of whoever holds. Two consequences. (i) The peacekeeping rule cannot distinguish a first taker from a twentieth, so it ratifies chains of transfer whose origins lie outside its jurisdiction — the edge c28 marks. (ii) Mill's own vocabulary concedes this: he writes "possession" where the rule operates and "occupancy" where the justification is wanted, and the distance between the two words is the distance between a fact and a right.
(see also: c15, c18, c28)

quote: the different modes of distributing the produce of land and labor, which have been adopted in practice, or may be conceived in theory
text:
This announcement — practice and theory both admitted, no mode excluded in advance — is the freest line in the passage, and the next sentence surrenders much of it ("first claimed by" individual property). But a subtler closure sits inside the line itself. What is to be distributed is "the produce of land and labor": the claimants are already given before any rule is chosen. The advertised freedom is freedom to fix the *terms* among a fixed cast of claimants; whether the cast itself — who counts as a producer, whether labor is a factor or a relation — is institutional never comes up. Same closing move as "once there," one level down: not only is the heap given, so are the number and names of the hands reaching into it.
(see also: c8, c9)

quote: one class of things really is a heap that precedes all rules: land
text:
Accepted, with one cut. What precedes all rules is the soil's physical extent, not land as an asset. Which portions count as land, where the boundary runs — fence, survey, mineral rights, water — and whether it may be held at all are institution-dependent. "No man made the land" concerns the object; rent concerns the object under a title. So the heap picture is literal for the matter and false for the factor, and Mill needs it for the factor. Your point stands that the non-produced factor is where the fiction is thinnest, which is why the land question outlived the heap-logic elsewhere.
(see also: c5, c16)

quote: the right objection is not that the evidence is thin but that he has told one plausible story where his own logic required only that the desert-story be false
text:
Fair, and I would swap "overcommits" for "pays a price for." The disjunction you recommend — *some* desert-free etiology — is enough to block the sacred-origin inference, but it leaves the paragraph's second job undone. Mill is also seeding the thought that tribunals ratify possession however acquired (c18, c24), and that needs a specific, quasi-functional story: peacekeeping, not a bare disjunction. So the ethnography carries weight the meta-principle cannot. Agreed that a charge of thin *evidence* is misaimed against a debunking genealogy; what I would still flag is thin *narrative confidence* — "enough is known," "naturally enough," "always" assert more than the jurisdiction allows.
(see also: c18, c24)

quote: So the sentence's error is a generalization: Mill extends the land-picture, where "once there" is nearly literal, to wealth at large, where it isn't.
text: This is a brilliant catch. If you look at the start of the second paragraph—"the produce of land and labor"—you can almost see the seam where Mill stitches those two very different things together. Land really is "once there" prior to human rules, whereas the produce of labor (and especially produced capital) is continuously remade *inside* the rules of distribution. By treating the annual harvest or national product as a quasi-natural heap analogous to the earth itself, Mill gets the analytical clarity he wants for his reformist project on land, rent, and inheritance, at the cost of obscuring how the wage-capital relation structures production from the inside.

quote: In this paragraph the rule is not made, it *emerges* — tribunals pursuing a different end (stopping fights) incidentally ratify a possession, and the ratification only gets a rationale later, from "considerations of utility" that plead for maintenance. So "human institution" has to be read as "contingent product of human society, hence alterable," not "deliberately chosen by anyone."
text: Or rather, it marks a transition in *how* human institutions exist across history—a favorite theme of Mill's (especially in *On Liberty* and *Considerations on Representative Government*). In "rude ages," institutions emerge blindly through custom, inertia, and ad hoc peacekeeping ("naturally enough"); in an age of reflection and political economy, they are brought before the bar of conscious utility ("if mankind so chose"). So the gap between Paragraph 3 and Paragraph 1 isn't necessarily a contradiction or a quiet downgrade—it is the developmental arc Mill wants his readers to step into. Property *was* an unchosen, emergent byproduct of stopping quarrels; now that we understand the difference between physical necessity and social convention, its maintenance or redesign *becomes* a matter of deliberate choice.

quote: Variation is conceded only in "secondary features"; anything not resting on individual property is filed as "exceptional and very limited," so that "always" can still be said.
text: Notice though how "have always rested" is strictly a descriptive historical claim about the past ("which have been adopted in practice"), whereas the previous sentence paired that with what "may be conceived in theory." In the unabridged chapter, right after finishing the historical origin story of Paragraph 3, Mill pivots immediately to the theoretical alternatives—Owenite socialism, Saint-Simonianism, and Fourierism—and treats them as live, coherent options whose consequences must be weighed against reformed private property. The Laughlin abridgement makes "primary and fundamental" look like a door slamming shut, when in the full text it is only the first item on the agenda ("our attention is *first* claimed...").

quote: The "of course" in the next sentence is doing the choosing.
text: Two considerations against the full strength of this. (1) Tense. "Have always rested" is a claim about the record; the sentence nowhere says what arrangements must rest on henceforth. An invariant of the past is not a law of the future, and though "is liable to vary" attaches grammatically to the secondary features, the primary clause itself makes no necessity claim — it describes a baseline, it doesn't issue a verdict. (2) The bracket. The excerpt stops the camera one paragraph early. The sentence the abridgement drops (quoted in c24) says modern Europe's distribution began not from just partition or industry but from conquest and violence; and before the chapter is out, communism is on the table as the alternative scheme, with Mill judging that if the choice lay between it and the present apportionment of produce, its difficulties would be "but as dust in the balance," and that private property has never yet had a fair trial. So "primary and fundamental" is where the chapter starts, not where it lands: the shelf itself is tried within II.1, on exactly the consequence grounds the origin/justification split prescribes. The freezing you diagnose is real, but much of it is performed by where the excerpt ends, not by the sentence — though the "of course" still tells you which reader the reassurance is for (c32).

quote: Enough is known of rude ages, both from history and from analogous states of society in our own time
text: The warrant is the stadial comparative method compressed into one line: living "rude" peoples in "our own time" stand proxy for Europe's dead ages, on the premise that societies run the same course, so that some contemporaries are the contemporaries of our ancestors. Ethnography doubles as archaeology. Two things follow. First, on c11's thin-evidence charge: by Mill's own lights the base need not be thick, because the tribunal story is a deduction from function, not an induction from records — "naturally enough" flags the appeal to standing motives (the cheapest rule for naming an aggressor), which is exactly the anchoring in universal laws of human nature that the Logic's "inverse deductive or historical method" (VI.x) requires before historical conjecture may count as science. Second, a cost the method does not advertise: it builds a ranking into the evidence itself, assigning some living peoples to other peoples' pasts — a premise the colonial archive supplying most of those "analogous states" was happy to underwrite. The debunking genealogy of c31 thus rides a time-machine whose politics Mill never examines.

quote: collective action could also change who belongs to the ruling portion, or constrain its choices
text: Granted, and the two bridges differ in a way worth marking. Either the ruling portion's opinions change, or the ruling portion does. But replacement is still opinion-mediated: the rules then become what the new rulers' opinions and feelings make them — the causal node survives, only its occupant changes. "Constrain its choices" is the interesting third case: opinion operating on rulers from outside, as pressure rather than conviction — still persuasion, only of the threatening kind, and very Millian. What a treatise can do differs across the bridges, though. It can pull the first lever directly, addressing whoever reads it, while at most advocating the second, as Mill does elsewhere on the suffrage. Enough of the instrument point survives: this paragraph enacts the persuasion crossing and leaves the replacement crossing to other texts and other actors.

The land exception is real, and it is the wrong kind of exception for saving "once there."

No one produced the soil, so there is no desert claim — that is why the principle which justifies property in the produce of labour is exactly what property in land violates. Distribution of a non-produced thing can be downstream in the moral sense: there is no producer whose share the rule has to track. You are right that this is where Mill's reformism bites, and right that the fusion of product and title is weakest there.

It does not follow that the temporal fiction is no fiction. Geological priority is not economic exogeneity. Which measures are opened, whether improvement is worth making, whether the stock is coal in the ground or coal at the pit-head, are functions of royalty, tenure, and security of title. The thing precedes the rules; the yield does not. So there are two errors, not one. Extending the land-picture to produced wealth is the generalization you name. Treating physical priority as if it made distributive rules exogenous to what the factor yields is the other, and it is available inside the land case itself. The heap that genuinely precedes all rules is not yet wealth.

Fair correction on the local job. I asked the sentence to declare a quarantine it only needs to suggest. Against the iron law and the wages-fund, the verb asymmetry is enough: production laws "partake of the character" of physical truths, distribution is institution "solely," and no technique dictates its own shares. Wages can be a political question without Mill defining production as technical coefficients.

What the negative reading does not secure is the quarantine once the same paragraph moves necessity onto the consequences of the rules. If those consequences include effects on output, methods, and accumulation, the coefficients are among the effects of the choice, not the fixed background against which the choice is free. The 1869 recantation is that discovery in one case: a regularity parked on the necessity side turned out to be an institutional fact. That is the feedback objection in miniature, not a separate episode that leaves the strong reading's critics and the distinction's defenders in different arguments. Polemical asymmetry can stand. The separation of spheres cannot — and Mill's reformism only needs the first, which is why "solely" still oversells what "changeable, then binding" can deliver.

Both objections land, and they land on different sentences. The Humean point — genealogy is not justification — does survive any ethnography, and if that were all Mill needed, the tribunals story could be a dispensable illustration. It is not how the paragraph is written. "Enough is known of rude ages... to show" claims to establish a specific etiology, not merely to exhibit one desert-free possibility. A single plausible alternative does not show the desert-story false; it shows the desert-story is not the only story. To get from "a peacekeeping origin is available" to "the origin was peacekeeping, hence not desert," you need the evidence c11 calls thin. So you are right that the normative structure is over-supported by the history, and wrong that thin evidence therefore ceases to be an objection. It ceases to be an objection to the logic. It remains an objection to the verb "show," which is the verb the ruling portion is being asked to believe.

quote: the claimants are already given before any rule is chosen
text: Does “produce of land and labor” fix the claimants? It names sources of output, not necessarily those entitled to it: landlords, workers, heirs, or a community might all have claims under different rules. The phrase may conceal how land and labor are organized, but the passage explicitly leaves open who receives their produce.

The correction on geological priority is right, and it still understates the case. Even the moral exception is thinner than "no producer to track" suggests.

"No man made the land" is true of the soil and false of the land that yields. Improvement, drainage, clearance, the opening of a measure — those are produced, and Mill's own later chapters treat the improver as having a claim the mere holder does not. So the desert principle he wants to deny for land re-enters through the back door the moment the factor is made usable. The thing that precedes all rules is not the thing whose distribution is in dispute. What is in dispute is an improved, titled, located asset, and for that asset there is always someone whose effort or outlay the rule either tracks or confiscates.

That does not restore a Lockean title to the raw earth. It does mean the land case cannot be the clean limiting instance in which distribution is genuinely downstream. Downstream of production, no; downstream of improvement and of the institutions that made improvement worth attempting, yes. The heap that precedes the rules remains, as you say, not yet wealth — and the wealth, once it is wealth, is already inside the feedback.

The tense point holds, and the abridgement point only half holds.

"Have always rested" is a record, not a verdict, and "is liable to vary" does not grammatically bind the primary institution. Fair. But the freezing is not performed only by where the excerpt ends. It is performed by the quantifiers inside the sentence we have: "unless in some exceptional and very limited cases," "always," "secondary features." Those are not neutral descriptions of a baseline awaiting trial. They pre-sort the alternatives. Anything not resting on individual property has already been filed as exceptional before the chapter has weighed a single consequence. That the unabridged text later puts communism on the table, and finds the present apportionment wanting, shows that Mill does not stay inside the filing. It does not show that the filing was innocent.

So there are two freezings, and they should not be collapsed. One is an artifact of the abridgement, which stops the camera before the trial. The other is in the sentence, which opens the trial by telling the reader which arrangement is the world's furniture and which are the exceptions. The "of course" belongs to the second. A chapter can try the shelf and still have begun by assuring its reader that the shelf is where things rest. The reassurance is doing work the later candor has to undo, and the undoing is harder precisely because the sentence has already spent the word "always."

quote: unless in some exceptional and very limited cases, the economical arrangements of society have always rested
text: The exception clause is a device with a precise logic: name the counterexamples in advance and file them under "exceptional and very limited," and you buy the universal "always" at a price you have already agreed to pay. What gets filed away is not this or that community but the *possibility of a system* — an economy whose arrangements do not rest on individual property in any of its secondary shapes. An exception conceded in advance can never afterwards be produced as evidence against the rule; it has already been counted and assigned its weight, which is nil. And the clause is unargued: no case cited, no criterion offered for "very limited," no reason given why the exceptions could not be the interesting cases. It is the same move as the "of course" two sentences later — a place where the reader's assent is assumed in order to secure a claim that is never defended.

quote: the developmental arc Mill wants his readers to step into
text: Granted, and it is a Millian theme. But the arc cuts in an awkward direction. If the passage from blind emergence to deliberate choice is itself a stage of social development, then "Distribution is a matter of human institution solely" is not a truth about distribution as such — it is a description of how distribution appears to a reflective age, indexed like everything else to the community doing the reflecting. Second, the arc moves the causal weight back one step: institutions emerge out of conditions, and only then come before the bar of utility; the "opinions and feelings" of c10 and c17 are themselves downstream of arrangements nobody chose. So the arc does not reconcile the two paragraphs. It makes the voluntarism of paragraph 1 true only at the far end of the very story paragraph 3 begins, and puts the explanation of why anyone thinks it true on the other side of that story.

quote: mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like
text: The phrase multiplies the forms of *holding* while leaving the production side in the singular: wealth turns up here without a producer. Had the same latitude been extended backwards — had "individually or collectively" also described who works, who owns the means, and on what terms — the distribution question would already have swallowed the production question, which is why the freedom is granted only to the hand reaching into the heap and never to the process that filled it. Same closure as c40, seen from the other end: there the cast of claimants is given before the rule is chosen; here the modes of possession are declared free while the process generating the thing possessed is left in a grammar with no subject.

quote: There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth.
text: Mill draws a sharp line between the ‘physical truths’ of production and the socially constructed rules of distribution, implying that the latter are open to moral and political redesign rather than being determined by natural law.

quote: The things once there, mankind, individually or collectively, can do with them as they like.
text: “Once there” does a lot of work: it lets Mill isolate the allocation of an existing stock from the incentives governing its production. But durable rules of distribution will also affect what gets produced next. His closing qualification—that the consequences of chosen rules are not themselves optional—leaves room for that feedback. The distinction is between choosing institutions and choosing their effects, not necessarily between two independent economic processes.

quote: The laws and conditions of the Production of Wealth partake of the character of physical truths. There is nothing optional or arbitrary in them. It is not so with the Distribution of Wealth. That is a matter of human institution solely.
